sections.h2: Which selling route fits a Lawrenceville homeowner?
sections.html:
Three paths are open to owners: hire a listing agent, sell without one, or take an as-is purchase. The house's shape and your move-out date usually decide. Lawrenceville is the seat of Gwinnett County, around 30 miles northeast of downtown Atlanta, and the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 32,822 residents.

Gwinnett is among Georgia's busiest property markets, so a tidy house with updated systems can draw several showings. A property carrying deferred repairs or a clouded title may close faster when the buyer brings cash.

sections.h2: How do Lawrenceville's homes and households compare in the Census?
sections.html:
Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 put a typical owner-occupied home value of $350,600 and typical gross rent of $1,613. Among 10,719 households, 47.0 percent own their home, and the average household holds 2.82 people.

  • Median household income: $61,561 (in 2024 dollars)
  • People who speak another language at home: 41.4 percent
  • Foreign-born residents: 29.5 percent
  • Average trip to work: 32.1 minutes

With more than four in ten residents using another language at home, marketing a listing in several languages can reach buyers an English-only ad would miss.

sections.h2: What is Lawrenceville's history and layout?
sections.html:
The General Assembly chartered Lawrenceville on December 15, 1821, the second oldest city in the metro area, and it honors Commodore James Lawrence of War of 1812 fame. The courthouse site on the square was chosen that year. The present courthouse there dates to 1885, and the Gwinnett Justice and Administration Center opened in 1988 and gained a new courthouse wing in 2020.

During the Civil War the county voted against secession, and the Lawrenceville Manufacturing Company cotton mill was burned by Union soldiers. Today the city spreads over about 13.5 square miles of central Gwinnett and touches Dacula, Buford, Suwanee, Duluth, Norcross, Lilburn, Snellville and Grayson. Streets near the square differ sharply from newer subdivisions, so ask which era your house belongs to before you price it.

sections.h2: What do buyers like about downtown Lawrenceville?
sections.html:
The historic square anchors the city. The Lawrenceville Arts Center, home of the Aurora Theatre, has a 500-seat theatre, a cabaret, a courtyard and a gallery, and it draws about 80,000 visitors a year. The Lawrenceville Lawn offers an amphitheater, dog park and walking path, and Rhodes Jordan Park covers 162 acres with a fishing lake, swim facilities and a 1.9-mile paved trail.

Three downtown buildings, the Old Seminary Building, the Isaac Adair House and the county courthouse, carry federal historic listings, and the Lawrenceville Heritage Trail runs through downtown. The city says it was named a Tree City in February 2023. If your house is a short walk from the square, lead the listing with those places.

sections.h2: What local work and roads support Lawrenceville home values?
sections.html:
Courts, clinics and classrooms employ a large part of the local workforce. Census data lists 2022 health care and social assistance receipts of about $2.2 billion alongside retail sales near $1.68 billion, a mix that suits a county seat with courts and clinics. Georgia Gwinnett College is within city limits, and the Presbyterian Church in America has kept its headquarters here since 1988.

State Route 316, U.S. 78 and U.S. 29 cross the area, and Ride Gwinnett and Xpress GA commuter buses serve the city. Gwinnett County Airport lies partly within Lawrenceville. With long commutes common, buyers weigh road access carefully.

Public education comes from Gwinnett County Public Schools. Inside the city are Benefield, Margaret Winn Holt, Jenkins and Lawrenceville elementaries, Jordan Middle, Central Gwinnett and Discovery high schools, and the Phoenix alternative school. Jenkins feeds Jordan and then Central Gwinnett, and Benefield feeds Richards Middle and then Discovery.

Some addresses are zoned to schools outside the limits, including Simonton and Cedar Hill elementaries, and one northern subdivision goes to Collins Hill High. Zoning follows the street address, so ask the district to confirm the assignment for a given house.

sections.h2: How are Lawrenceville property taxes billed?
sections.html:
Since tax year 2021 the city has billed its own property tax, so sellers see two bills: Gwinnett County's and the City Finance Department's. The city's 2026 millage rate is 3.26 mills, where each mill means one dollar of tax per thousand of assessed value. Assessed value is 40 percent of the fair market value set by the Gwinnett Board of Assessors.

City residents with a homestead get $20,000 knocked off assessed value, except on debt service levies. Bills paid late draw monthly interest at the prime rate plus 3 percent, and a 5 percent penalty lands every 120 days until it reaches 20 percent. The due date comes from Finance at 678-407-6675. Have the closing attorney check both bills.

sections.h2: How do I claim a Gwinnett homestead exemption?
sections.html:
The Gwinnett Tax Commissioner takes applications until April 1, and the house must have been your primary residence on January 1 of that year. The county's notice says nothing is granted automatically, and a granted exemption need not be renewed. You can apply online at GwinnettTaxCommissioner.com/apply.

A sale ends your exemption, and the buyer will need to apply separately.

Planning and Development issues permits through the Licensing, Permits and Plans portal, and registering there costs nothing. Electrical, mechanical, plumbing, occupancy and structural jobs each call for a building permit. A Certificate of Occupancy must come first when a building's use changes.

Permits go only to a buildable lot of record, meaning land recorded in Gwinnett's court records before June 2, 1970, or shown on an approved, recorded plat. Sewer, water and septic permits are issued by Gwinnett County. Planning and Development, at 678-407-6583, can tell you about any open permit.

sections.h2: Do weather and drainage matter for a Lawrenceville sale?
sections.html:
Yes, an inspection will cover both. Annual rainfall here is close to 53.5 inches, July afternoons average 91 degrees, and the record high is 104. Drainage around the foundation, gutter condition and attic ventilation are the items buyers' inspectors check first.

The city's tax bill can also carry a stormwater fee, which pays for drainage structures the city maintains and is distinct from the county water bill. Check that line on the bill so a buyer sees the full annual cost of owning the property.

faqs.q: Does the City of Lawrenceville send its own tax bill?
faqs.a: Yes, since tax year 2021. The Gwinnett County bill no longer includes the city tax, and Finance answers questions at 678-407-6675.

faqs.q: What is the city's 2026 millage rate?
faqs.a: 3.26 mills, a levy of $3.26 on each $1,000 of assessed value. It covers the city levy only, not county or school taxes.

faqs.q: What is the last day to apply for a Gwinnett homestead exemption?
faqs.a: April 1. Ownership and residence on January 1 are required, and approved exemptions stay in place without yearly reapplication.

faqs.q: Can a house with unpaid city tax still be sold?
faqs.a: Usually, with the balance taken from proceeds at closing. Georgia law allows a FiFa lien on unpaid tax, so settle it before accepting an offer.

faqs.q: Must I get a permit before selling?
faqs.a: The permit triggers the city lists are construction-type work, not a sale. Open permits can still hold up a buyer's loan or title review, so confirm with Planning and Development that old jobs were closed.
